summary: Defines the starting principles and policy for the tpc.int subdomain, a set of service listings reachable over the Internet through a name space within the Domain Name System.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1530 sets up tpc.int, a part of the Domain Name System where telephone numbers are written as names. A host that offers to print or fax for you registers itself under that name, and the memo explains who may join, how the policy is settled, and who decides.

questions: how does tpc.int map phone numbers to hosts
what is the board of arbitration and conciliation
subtitle: The founding rules for tpc.int, a corner of the DNS that maps telephone numbers to hosts willing to print or fax for you.

tldr.problem: A fax machine plugged into the telephone network cannot be reached over the Internet, so nobody could send it a message without a private arrangement.
tldr.mechanism: The tpc.int subdomain puts telephone numbers into the Domain Name System as MX resource records, so that a name server can answer with the hosts that are willing to print or fax for a given number, and the policy for that namespace is set by a board drawn from the sites that provide the service.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that specifies no standard, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

facts.label: Board terms
facts.value: Two years, with half or more of the initial Board serving one year

today: RFC 1530 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out the first principles of a subdomain of the DNS that mapped telephone numbers to hosts willing to print or fax for you, and it hands the policy for that namespace to a board of five named members.

sections.title: What the tpc.int Subdomain Is For
sections.content:
The memo defines the initial principles of operation for the tpc.int subdomain, a collection of service listings reachable over the Internet through an administered namespace inside the Domain Name System. It is informational and applies only to the Internet sites that choose to register themselves there. The subdomain is organised as a cooperative of the sites that provide access within it, and policy for the subdomain is set by a board responsible to that cooperative.

The primary purpose is to provide a transparent mapping between general-purpose computers on the Internet and special-purpose devices connected directly to the telephone network. This extends the population reachable from the Internet by giving a communications path to devices that are not otherwise directly addressable.

The service defined first is remote printing, which ties together G3-compatible facsimile devices on the telephone network with users of electronic mail on the Internet and with the message-handling domains that connect to the Internet through application-layer gateways. The memo is careful to say that remote printer gateways had long been technically feasible and had become an integral part of many individual networks. What tpc.int adds is a common namespace, which transforms remote printing from a single-site, value-added service into an integral transparent service in the global Internet.

The remote printing facility is built on top of the electronic mail protocols of the Internet, including RFC 822 and MIME. Because it uses the message-handling facilities of the Internet, the service is also available to message-handling domains connected to the Internet through application-layer gateways, naming X.400-compatible systems, UUCP-based message-handling environments, and commercial services such as AT&T Mail, MCI Mail, SprintMail and CompuServe.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is simple. A telephone number is written as a name in the DNS, and the DNS then points to the computers that are willing to send a fax on your behalf. The fax itself travels over the telephone network, but the request travels over the Internet, so anyone with mail access can reach it.

sections.title: How a Telephone Number Becomes a DNS Name
sections.content:
Services in the Internet are identified with a service target name listed in the DNS. Those target names are looked up in the DNS and the resource records associated with the name are returned. After the name lookup has been completed, the initiator exchanges a series of IP packets with an Internet site that provides access to a service reachable through the tpc.int subdomain.

For remote printing, the DNS MX resource record is used to register the Internet sites that provide access to the facility. A site running a remote printer server registers itself in the DNS as willing to provide access to some portion of the telephone system numbering plan, registered by one or more MX records inside the tpc.int subdomain. The memo's worked example is a host named hewes.radio.com that is willing to print for devices whose telephone numbers begin with the prefix +1-415-336; the host is then listed with an MX record whose target name is the telephone number written backwards, one digit per label, with a wildcard at the front.

The resource records can have an arbitrary level of precision. The North American numbering plan, country code 1, is structured by a 3-digit area code, then a 3-digit exchange prefix, then a 4-digit station number, and the memo shows records at each of those levels: one that reaches any printer in area code 415, another that reaches any printer in area code 415 with exchange prefix 968, and one that could be used if all the printers in an organisation shared the prefix +1-415-96. The level of precision is a matter of choice rather than of rule.
sections.plainLanguage: The telephone number is turned into a DNS name by writing it backwards, one digit per label. The more digits you include, the narrower the group of printers it reaches, and the site picks how precise to be.

sections.title: Registering Sites Without Bias
sections.content:
It is the responsibility of the administrators of the tpc.int namespace to register only those Internet sites that are willing to confirm to the principles of operation as defined in the memo and as periodically amended by the Board of Arbitration and Conciliation.

The memo then states a key principle. All Internet sites that meet the principles of operation shall be registered in the tpc.int subdomain without bias, and the subdomain should encourage the largest number of Internet sites possible.

What happens when more than one site wants to serve the same area is handled by keeping multiple resource records for the same target name. The DNS returns those records in an unordered list, but in practice the initiator consults the list in the order it was returned. To keep the environment unbiased, an authoritative name server for the tpc.int subdomain shall alternate the ordering of the list frequently, and shall return a small TTL with the resource records, so that no site can rely on being chosen first.
sections.plainLanguage: Any site that meets the rules gets in, and the memo wants as many sites as possible. When several serve the same area, the name server shuffles the list each time so that no one of them is always picked.

sections.title: The Board of Arbitration and Conciliation
sections.content:
Policies for the tpc.int subdomain are determined by its Board of Arbitration and Conciliation. The memo explains where the idea comes from: it has its roots in English law, which permitted the members of a trade to appoint masters and workmen among them to serve as councils of arbitration and conciliation for matters incapable of being otherwise settled. The Board in tpc.int consists of members of the cooperative, appointed to hear and determine all questions between members which may be submitted to them arising out of the operation of services listed in the subdomain.

The initial Board is defined in the memo itself. Members serve two-year terms, except that 50 percent or more of the initial Board shall serve a one-year term. The Board shall determine and publish procedures that allow members of the cooperative to select new members of the Board as their terms expire.

If an issue relating to the definition of a service, or to the operation of a service listed in the subdomain, is raised and cannot be settled otherwise, a member submits the matter to the Board. The Board hears the question, makes provisions for comments by other members of the cooperative and by the general public, and makes and publishes a determination of policy.

Secretariat services for the subdomain are initially provided by the Internet Multicasting Service, a non-profit corporation located in Washington, D.C., and the cooperative may contract with other groups for the provision of those services at any time. The subdomain is organised as a cooperative so that policy determination stays in the hands of those offering the services, and the memo says the aim is a large number of sites, combining the distributed local efforts of many individuals and small groups into a global service.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are made by a board of five people drawn from the sites that provide the service, in the style of an English trade arbitration council. The board settles any question the members cannot settle between themselves and publishes its decisions.

sections.title: Other Subdomains and the First Board Members
sections.content:
The memo notes that other logical subdomains may be established to provide similar mappings. The Internet sites taking part in those other subdomains might also be registered under tpc.int, or might choose to be registered solely within those other subdomains, under different policies. It is the policy of the tpc.int cooperative to encourage the establishment of other service listing domains, whether as a public trust or cooperative or as a purely commercial venture.

The initial Board of Arbitration and Conciliation is listed in the memo: Dr Rob Blokzijl of NIKHEF in Amsterdam, the Netherlands; Dr Jun Murai of Keio University in Fujisawa, Japan; Geoff Huston of AARNET in Canberra, Australia; Dr Marshall T. Rose of Dover Beach Consulting in Mountain View, California; and Carl Malamud of the Internet Multicasting Service in Washington, D.C.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo leaves room for other namespaces with their own rules, and names the five people who start the board. It says nothing about security.
